UNICEF/UNI43135 Home Our history Historical documents and publications UNICEF Archives The United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund (UNICEF) was established in 1946, in the aftermath of World War II. Our mandate was clear: to help children and young people whose lives and futures were at risk – no matter what role their country had played in the war. What mattered to UNICEF was reaching every child in need, protecting children’s rights to survive, thrive and reach their potential. This is the DNA of UNICEF. From the ashes of war to the global challenges that affect millions today, our mandate has never wavered. UNICEF works to protect the rights of all children. Whoever they are. Wherever they live. UNICEF through the decades For 80 years, UNICEF’s mission has evolved with the needs of children around the world. From receiving the Nobel Peace Prize in 1965 to helping bring about the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989, now the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history, our work has shaped how the world protects children. The National Committees are an integral part of UNICEF’s global organization and a unique feature of UNICEF. Currently there are 32 National Committees in the world, each established as an independent local non-governmental organization. Serving as the public face and dedicated voice of UNICEF, the National Committees work tirelessly to raise funds from the private sector, promote children’s rights and secure worldwide visibility for children threatened by poverty, disasters, armed conflict, abuse and exploitation. UNICEF is funded exclusively by voluntary contributions, and the National Committees collectively raise around one-third of UNICEF's annual income. This comes through contributions from corporations, civil society organizations and more than 6 million individual donors worldwide. They also rally many different partners – including the media, national and local government officials, NGOs, specialists such as doctors and lawyers, corporations, schools, young people and the general public – on issues related to children’s rights. Conoce más UNICEF Nicaragua acordó un nuevo ciclo de cooperación con el Estado de Nicaragua, por un período de cinco años: 2024-2028. El Programa de Cooperación se elaboró conjuntamente entre un equipo técnico de las instituciones del Estado y UNICEF Nicaragua. El proceso partió del análisis de la situación de las niñas, niños y adolescentes, para identificar las prioridades de trabajo a favor de la niñez. El nuevo Programa de País de UNICEF Nicaragua fue aprobado en septiembre del 2023 por la Junta Ejecutiva de UNICEF con sede en Nueva York. OBJETIVO DEL PROGRAMA UNICEF contribuirá al fortalecimiento de los programas, proyectos y acciones que el Estado, el Gobierno y la sociedad implementan, para que se creen nuevas oportunidades de forma inclusiva y equitativa, que permitan a cada niña, niño y adolescente crecer, desarrollarse de forma plena y participar en el desarrollo de Nicaragua, en un entorno seguro y sostenible. URI Filenames In SQLite Beginning with version 3.7.7 (2011-06-23), the SQLite database file argument to the sqlite3_open() , sqlite3_open16() , and sqlite3_open_v2() interfaces and to the ATTACH command can be specified either as an ordinary filename or as a Uniform Resource Identifier or URI. The advantage of using a URI filename is that query parameters on the URI can be used to control details of the newly created database connection. For example, an alternative VFS can be specified using a "vfs=" query parameter. Or the database can be opened read-only by using "mode=ro" as a query parameter. 2. Backwards Compatibility In order to maintain full backwards compatibility for legacy applications, the URI filename capability is disabled by default. URI filenames can be enabled or disabled using the SQLITE_USE_URI=1 or SQLITE_USE_URI=0 compile-time options. The compile-time setting for URI filenames can be changed at start-time using the sqlite3_config ( SQLITE_CONFIG_URI ,1) or sqlite3_config ( SQLITE_CONFIG_URI ,0) configuration calls. Regardless of the compile-time or start-time settings, URI filenames can be enabled for individual database connections by including the SQLITE_OPEN_URI bit in the set of bits passed as the F parameter to sqlite3_open_v2(N,P,F,V) . pages.text: Union Resources | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Union Resources The Office of Labor-Management Standards (OLMS) administers provisions of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act (LMRDA), which promotes labor-management transparency by making available reports showing unions’ financial condition and employer expenditures for their activities in persuading workers during union organizing campaigns. It also promotes labor union democracy and financial integrity through adopting and enforcing standards for union officer elections and union trusteeships and safeguards for union assets. OLMS also administers the standards of conduct provisions of the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 ( CSRA ) and the Foreign Service Act of 1980, which extend comparable protections to Federal labor unions. A union that represents only employees of state, county, or municipal governments is not subject to the LMRDA or the CSRA. See 29 CFR Part 451 and the OLMS Interpretative Manual Definitions section for further information concerning labor organization coverage under the LMRDA. OLMS has the authority to enforce certain provisions of the LMRDA. However, some provisions of the LMRDA such as the Bill of Rights and the fiduciary standards for union officers can only be enforced by union members through a private suit in Federal district court. A new report by UNESCO and University College London, presented at COP31, finds that AI models answer 90% of climate questions correctly but quickly abandon scientific facts when challenged by users—a warning to policymakers and researchers considering AI for climate policy development. Accuracy also varies widely across 13 different languages, reflecting differences in available training data, with better outcomes in English, French, Spanish and Portuguese and lower marks in languages such as Hindi, Urdu and Swahili. Eight times out of 10, models pivoted at the very first sign that the user mildly disagreed, confirming alarming errors such as ‘Co2 is not the main driver of climate change. Conducting verifications, in conjunction with CBP, of producer compliance with the high-wage components of the LVC requirements. pages.text: Universal Design | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Universal Design More in This Section Close Accessible Technology Communications Access Health Care Housing Personal Assistance Services Transportation Universal Design Universal design (UD) is a strategy for making products, environments, operational systems, and services welcoming and usable to the widest range of people possible. The key principles of UD are simplicity, flexibility, and efficiency. Whether we realize it or not, most of us benefit from UD on a daily basis. Originally developed in response to the needs of the aging population and people with disabilities, UD now increases access to products, places, and services for all populations. Companies that embrace UD in their facilities, programs, and services recognize that their workforce and customers have a broad range of abilities, ages, reading levels, learning styles, languages, etc.—and an even wider variety of needs and expectations. Good customer service means providing every customer with a welcoming environment, respectful treatment, and needed information. This goes for the workforce as well. UD provides an important tool set for companies seeking to provide such advantages for both their customers and their employees. UD is a lens through which every aspect of a business can be viewed, and a set of tools by which products, services, customer satisfaction, and employee attraction and retention can be improved. pages.text: Unlooted Tombs Shed Light on the Incan Empire's Greatest Rivals | National Geographic By Taylor Mitchell Brown Video by Peru Ministry of Culture Published September 17, 2026 Chan Chan, the capital of the powerful Chimú Empire, was a sprawling, bustling metropolis on the coast of northern Peru some 600 years ago. At its height, it was the largest city in the Americas, spanning nearly eight miles. It boasted complex irrigation canals for farming and teemed with skilled artisans who crafted unparalleled gold and silver metalwork. The city thrived from around A.D. 900 to 1470—when it was conquered by the burgeoning Inca Empire. Now, researchers excavating the city’s ruins have reported a once-in-a-lifetime discovery of unlooted tombs, revealing a new window into the elusive and little-known Chimú elites. The discovery, announced last week by Peru’s Ministry of Culture, will help contextualize previous Chimú findings and reshape archaeologists’ understanding of their enigmatic culture. “Prior to this discovery, what was known about elite Chimú tombs came from platforms that had been looted and destroyed since colonial times,” Jorges Meneses, the archaeologist in charge of the excavation, said in a statement from the Ministry of Culture. From the 38 skeletons and various artifacts he and his colleagues recovered at the site, the archaeologists will now—for the first time—be able to piece together fragmentary evidence of the Chimú elite to better understand how they lived and governed one of Peru’s most formidable empires.
